statements.body: The operator runs a fleet of exactly four delivery vans.
Maintenance records are currently stored in a physical glovebox folder kept inside each individual van.
Services are being missed under the current paper-based system.
Centralising maintenance records into a single digital location will prevent services from being missed.
What types of maintenance records need to be tracked (e.g. oil changes, tyre rotations, MOT, annual inspections)?
Who is responsible for logging maintenance events — drivers, a fleet manager, or a third-party garage?
How should upcoming or overdue services be surfaced — dashboard, email alerts, SMS, or another mechanism?
Whether historical records from the glovebox folders will be migrated into the new system has not been decided.

concerns.coverage: Maintenance records are siloed per van in physical glovebox folders, causing services to be missed; the pain is felt today by whoever manages the four-van fleet.
The idea is written from the perspective of a single operator managing four vans; no other roles (drivers, mechanics, administrators) have been named yet.
Records currently live in a per-van physical folder; no capture process, handoff sequence, or exit point for a digital workflow has been described.
The data in scope is vehicle maintenance records; exact record types, volume, structure, and retention or export requirements are not yet stated.
Success is framed as services no longer being missed; no measurable threshold or observable behaviour change beyond that has been specified.

candidates.body: Who will actually enter each maintenance event into the system at the moment work is done — a driver at the van, you at a desk later, or the garage?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger already flags logging responsibility as an unknown, and it is the single point of failure for the whole idea: if nobody owns the capture step, the digital folder goes stale exactly like the glovebox folders did. Answering it names the primary operator and defines where the first vertical slice's workflow begins.

candidates.body: How do you determine that a service is due for a van — fixed mileage intervals, calendar dates, manufacturer schedules, or something else?
candidates.whySelected: Services cannot be flagged as upcoming or overdue without knowing what 'due' is derived from; this bounds the core data model (does the system need odometer readings?) and directly tests whether centralised records alone can prevent misses.

candidates.body: When a service becomes due or overdue, what single mechanism would you actually notice and act on — a screen you already check, an email, or an SMS?
candidates.whySelected: This resolves the approved unknown about surfacing and the tension between the hypothesis that centralisation prevents misses and the fact that no reminder path exists yet; a store with no active surfacing may just be a digital glovebox.

contradictions.summary: The hypothesis that centralising records into one digital location will prevent missed services sits in tension with the still-open question of how upcoming or overdue services are surfaced: without an agreed surfacing mechanism, a central store may reproduce the passive-folder failure mode that causes misses today.

readyAdvice.why: All core concerns have some coverage, but the capture ownership, due-date logic, and surfacing mechanism are all still unknowns; a first vertical slice cannot be bounded until at least the capture step has a named owner and 'due' has a definition.

statements.body: Success requires zero overdue services across all four vans for a full calendar quarter.
The system must be able to produce a complete printable maintenance history for any individual van, intended for use at point of sale.
Selling a van is an anticipated event that makes exportable per-vehicle history a near-term rather than speculative requirement.

concerns.coverage: Two concrete, observable success criteria have been named: no overdue services across the fleet for a full quarter, and the ability to print a full van history on demand at point of sale.

A full printable maintenance history per van is required, implying records must be retained for the working life of each vehicle and exportable in a human-readable format; no record types or volume have been added yet.
No exclusions stated, but the point-of-sale history requirement implies record completeness is in scope, not just forward-looking alerts — a boundary worth making explicit in a later pass.

candidates.body: Will the historical maintenance records currently in the glovebox folders be entered into the new system before any vans are put up for sale?
candidates.whySelected: The approved requirement for a complete printable history at point of sale (586edb0f, 618b5acc) cannot be met without the paper history, yet migration is explicitly undecided (7116dfda). Resolving this determines whether the first slice includes a data-entry effort and how much of the past must be captured, so it collapses the largest live tension in the ledger.

candidates.body: Who will actually log each maintenance event when it happens — you, the drivers, or the garage that does the work?
candidates.whySelected: The user concern coverage notes no operator role beyond the owner has been named, and an approved unknown (dfded80e) already flags this. Naming the person who does capture defines the workflow entry point and who the first slice must be usable for.

candidates.body: Which specific maintenance record types must the system track from day one?
candidates.whySelected: An approved unknown (d21da8e4) names this gap; record types define the data model for the first slice and what counts toward the zero-overdue-services success criterion, though it bounds the slice less sharply than resolving migration.

contradictions.summary: The system must produce a complete printable maintenance history per van for point of sale, and selling a van is a near-term event, but whether the existing paper records will be migrated has not been decided — without migration, no history produced by the new system can be complete.

readyAdvice.why: All ten core concerns have at least some coverage and success is measurable, but the migration decision directly gates an approved near-term requirement, and the capture role and record types remain open — the first slice cannot be confidently bounded until at least the migration question is answered.

statements.body: Drivers log a maintenance issue or mileage reading when they park up at the end of a run.
The fleet operator reviews upcoming services on a weekly cadence and books the garage.
Completed maintenance work is entered into the record from the garage invoice after the service is done.
The maintenance logging workflow has three distinct roles and steps: driver capture at park-up, operator weekly review and booking, and operator post-service entry from invoice.

concerns.coverage: Three roles are now named in the workflow: drivers (who log issues and mileage), the fleet operator (who reviews, books, and enters completed work), and the garage (whose invoices are the source of truth for completed work).

Work enters the system at two driver-side capture points (issue or mileage at park-up); the operator reviews weekly, triggers a garage booking, then closes the loop by entering completed work from the invoice. The garage itself is an external handoff point, not a system user.

candidates.body: Which specific maintenance record types must the system track from day one — for example scheduled services, MOT/inspections, tyre changes, repairs, and mileage logs?
candidates.whySelected: This is the last open unknown that directly shapes the data model. Every workflow step is now defined (driver capture, weekly review, invoice entry), but none of it can be built until the record types those steps carry are named. It also bounds the printable van history, since a 'complete' history is only complete relative to a known set of record types.

candidates.body: When the operator does their weekly review, how do they want upcoming and overdue services surfaced — a dashboard they open, or an alert pushed to them by email or SMS?
candidates.whySelected: The weekly review is the step that actually prevents missed services, so the surfacing mechanism is the heart of the success criterion. It remains an approved unknown and choosing between pull (dashboard) and push (alerts) meaningfully changes what the first slice must include.

candidates.body: Are there hard constraints on how this is built or hosted — such as budget, an existing tool it must live in (e.g. a spreadsheet), or who is available to maintain it?
candidates.whySelected: No environmental limits have been stated yet. A four-van operation may have very different tolerance for hosting cost and maintenance burden than a typical software project, and a stated constraint could invalidate an otherwise sensible slice.

readyAdvice.why: Workflow, roles, and success criteria are well established, but the record types the system must hold remain an approved unknown. A first slice cannot define its data model or its printable history without that answer; one more round should close it.
